title: Null-Space Filtering for Data-Free Continual Model Merging
one_liner: When merging multiple specialized models into one, filter out the overlapping changes to prevent forgetting old knowledge while learning new skills.
lead: Companies often fine-tune large models separately for different tasks: one for customer support, one for product recommendations, one for content moderation. Someday you need a single model that can handle all of them. Data-free continual model merging tries to fuse these independent models into one evolving backbone without looking back at the original training data. NUFILT does this by using null-space filtering: it mathematically identifies which parts of each new task's changes overlap with earlier tasks' changes, filters those overlapping parts out, then adds only the truly fresh signals needed for the new task.

problem.h2: The merging trap: grow or keep what you have
paras: You train a large model on one task and it works well. Then you train the same model on a second task and it works too, but now it forgets the first task (this is called catastrophic forgetting). A naive solution is to average the two trained models together, but averaging makes both tasks worse — the weights land in a zone that satisfies neither task's learned patterns.

The harder version: merge multiple fine-tuned models into one shared backbone that keeps growing with new tasks, without ever seeing the original training data again. Existing approaches try to keep the backbone "transparent" (remember old tasks) but end up too rigid to adapt to new ones, or they adapt well but trash the old knowledge.

callout.html: Merging independently trained models without data requires a way to identify which parts of each new task matter and which parts just re-learn old skills.

steps.text: For each new task, compute what changed in the model weights from the base model.
Identify which directions in weight space that task change shares with all earlier tasks, using the null space.
Remove those overlapping components from the new task change so it only contains fresh, new signals.
Train a small LoRA layer (a low-rank change) that injects the filtered-down task signals, preserving earlier knowledge.
Fold the adapter updates back into the backbone using simple layer-wise averaging, no extra counters or components remain.

paras: NUFILT changes which directions in weight space are allowed to move when a new task arrives. Instead of letting the new task update weights anywhere, it restricts updates to a carefully chosen subspace: the null space of earlier task changes. A task change is the difference in weights between the base model and the model after fine-tuning on one task. This mathematically enforces that new learning cannot interfere with patterns learned before.

hidden.h2: The null space: which directions are safe to move
hidden.name: null space of earlier task changes
paras: The null space is a set of directions in weight space that point sideways (perpendicular in high dimensions) to all the changes that earlier tasks made. When you restrict a new task's weight updates to this space, you mathematically guarantee those updates cannot disturb the patterns that old tasks learned. The paper estimates this by collecting all the earlier task changes — the differences between the base model weights and the weights after fine-tuning on each earlier task — and finding the directions orthogonal to them.

A task change is the raw direction a fine-tuned model moved from the base model. NUFILT projects new task changes onto the orthogonal complement (the null space) to identify which components are truly separate and different. The paper proves these task changes approximately align with learned representation patterns, justifying why null-space filtering preserves earlier knowledge while allowing new learning.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger presence in the null space (safe to move without disturbing earlier tasks).

reads.html: The null space is the set of all directions you can move in weight space without changing how the model responds to any earlier tasks.
Null-space filtering enforces transparency by projecting new task changes onto the orthogonal complement computed from the earlier task changes.

mechanism.h2: Why filtering preserves old knowledge while enabling new learning
paras: Old fine-tuned models have learned to respond to data in certain ways. Those response patterns live in the weights, but they live in specific directions of weight space — directions that task changes from old tasks point toward. A new task change, if you apply it directly, might move weights in those same directions, clobbering the old behavior.

NUFILT computes which directions are orthogonal to all earlier task changes (the null space). By restricting the new task's weight updates to only this space, the algorithm guarantees zero movement in the dangerous directions. The backbone remains transparent: it responds to the old tasks the same way as before. To enable the new task, a lightweight LoRA adapter (a small layer of low-rank weight changes) is then trained. This adapter is trained with a loss function that penalizes any changes that would contradict earlier knowledge, so it learns to work within constraints set by the filtered signals. The backbone stays intact and the new adapter adds capability without collision, because it only accesses the clean null-space directions.

Finally, the adapter is merged back into the backbone using layer-wise linear averaging, which turns a temporary piece into a permanent part of the model without increasing the weight count or the cost to run inference. The whole architecture stays streamlined: new knowledge enters through null-space updates and a trained adapter, earlier knowledge never moves, and the final merge is clean.

stages.s: Compute null space orthogonal to earlier changes
Project new task change onto null space
Train LoRA adapter with filtered signals
Merge adapter into backbone via averaging

math.words: The new task change is projected onto the null space of stacked earlier task changes, retaining only the orthogonal component.
symbols: the new task change (weight differences from fine-tuning on the new task)
rectangular block stacking all earlier task changes as rows
identity matrix (do nothing in all directions)
projection onto the subspace spanned by earlier task changes
projection onto the null space (the orthogonal complement)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose an earlier task moved weights in direction A by amount 1.0.
The new task wants to move in direction A by 0.4 and direction B by 0.6.
Null-space filtering removes the A component: 0.4 * (1 - 1) = 0.0.
Result: filtered task change is (0.0, 0.6). Only fresh, separate learning remains.

math.note: This projection mathematically guarantees that moving in the filtered directions does not contradict any earlier task's learned patterns.

items.b: Poor null-space estimate if task changes are noisy.
items.html: If the task changes are computed from sparse or small data, the orthogonal directions you filter to may not actually protect earlier knowledge. The projection becomes unreliable.
The LoRA adapter is deliberately lightweight to avoid extra counters. If the new task requires major structural changes, the adapter rank may be insufficient and performance drops.

items.b: Alignment assumption breaks if tasks are very different.
items.html: NUFILT assumes task changes align with learned representation patterns. If a new task is so different that it requires learning in entirely new representational zones, the filtering may throw away important signals.

items.b: Done right: compute task changes carefully, choose adapter rank to match task diversity, validate on representative new tasks.
items.html: Use enough data to estimate task changes accurately, profile the adapter rank against validation sets, and test the merged model thoroughly on new tasks you did not see during training.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple fine-tuning scenario: take a base vision model (or language model), fine-tune it on task 1 (e.g. cats vs dogs), then task 2 (e.g. vehicles). Compute task vectors for each. Implement null-space filtering: stack task 1's vector, compute its orthogonal complement, project task 2's vector onto that null space, and train a LoRA adapter with the filtered direction. Merge the adapter back into the base model. Measure accuracy on both tasks before and after merging.
demo.metric_eq: forgetting = accuracy_task1_after_merge - accuracy_task1_on_finetune, adaptation_gap = accuracy_task2_on_finetune - accuracy_task2_after_merge
demo.closing: The demo must show near-zero forgetting on task 1 while keeping task 2 accuracy close to independent fine-tuning — filtering works when both old and new skills remain sharp in a single model.
